text: Plants with soft, non-woody stems are called **herbs**. Many are small, such as mint, coriander and tomato, but height alone does not define a herb.

text: A banana plant is a large herb. Its trunk-like structure is a **pseudostem**, made from tightly overlapping leaf bases rather than a woody trunk. Its height does not make it a tree.

text: Some plants have stems that are too weak to stand. So they climb up something else — a wall, a fence, a stick, or another plant. These are called **climbers**. A money plant is a climber. So is a grape vine.

html: <text class="se-copy" x="542" y="732"><tspan x="542">Other plants also have weak stems. text: Other plants also have weak stems. But instead of climbing, they spread flat along the ground. These are called **creepers**. Pumpkin and watermelon plants are creepers.

<text class="se-copy" data-measure="874" x="89" y="968"><tspan x="89">Climbing<tspan data-gap="" dx="6.79553"> </tspan>and<tspan data-gap="" dx="6.79553"> </tspan>trailing<tspan data-gap="" dx="6.79553"> </tspan>describe<tspan data-gap="" dx="6.79553"> </tspan>growth<tspan data-gap="" dx="6.79553"> </tspan>habits,<tspan data-gap="" dx="6.79553"> </tspan>not<tspan data-gap="" dx="6.79553"> </tspan>a<tspan data-gap="" dx="6.79553"> </tspan>separate<tspan data-gap="" dx="6.79553"> </tspan>woody/non-woody</tspan><tspan x="89" dy="31">division.<tspan data-gap="" dx="1.37879"> </tspan>A<tspan data-gap="" dx="1.37879"> </tspan>grape<tspan data-gap="" dx="1.37879"> </tspan>vine<tspan data-gap="" dx="1.37879"> </tspan>is<tspan data-gap="" dx="1.37879"> </tspan>a<tspan data-gap="" dx="1.37879"> </tspan>woody<tspan data-gap="" dx="1.37879"> </tspan>climber;<tspan data-gap="" dx="1.37879"> </tspan>a<tspan data-gap="" dx="1.37879"> </tspan>pumpkin<tspan data-gap="" dx="1.37879"> </tspan>has<tspan data-gap="" dx="1.37879"> </tspan>non-woody<tspan data-gap="" dx="1.37879"> </tspan>trailing<tspan data-gap="" dx="1.37879"> </tspan>stems.</tspan><tspan x="89" dy="31">A plant can therefore be described in more than one way.</tspan></text>
text: Climbing and trailing describe growth habits, not a separate woody/non-woody division. A grape vine is a woody climber; a pumpkin has non-woody trailing stems. A plant can therefore be described in more than one way.

text: Hold a leaf up against the light. You will see thin lines running through it. These lines are **veins**. The pattern the veins make is called **venation**.

html: <text class="se-copy" data-measure="874" x="89" y="250"><tspan x="89">Veins<tspan data-gap="" dx="6.10071"> </tspan>contain<tspan data-gap="" dx="6.10071"> </tspan>tissues<tspan data-gap="" dx="6.10071"> </tspan>that<tspan data-gap="" dx="6.10071"> </tspan>transport<tspan data-gap="" dx="6.10071"> </tspan>water<tspan data-gap="" dx="6.10071"> </tspan>and<tspan data-gap="" dx="6.10071"> </tspan>dissolved<tspan data-gap="" dx="6.10071"> </tspan>substances.<tspan data-gap="" dx="6.10071"> </tspan>They<tspan data-gap="" dx="6.10071"> </tspan>carry</tspan><tspan x="89" dy="31">water<tspan data-gap="" dx="1.32199"> </tspan>into<tspan data-gap="" dx="1.32199"> </tspan>the<tspan data-gap="" dx="1.32199"> </tspan>leaf<tspan data-gap="" dx="1.32199"> </tspan>and<tspan data-gap="" dx="1.32199"> </tspan>sugars<tspan data-gap="" dx="1.32199"> </tspan>made<tspan data-gap="" dx="1.32199"> </tspan>in<tspan data-gap="" dx="1.32199"> </tspan>the<tspan data-gap="" dx="1.32199"> </tspan>leaf<tspan data-gap="" dx="1.32199"> </tspan>to<tspan data-gap="" dx="1.32199"> </tspan>other<tspan data-gap="" dx="1.32199"> </tspan>parts<tspan data-gap="" dx="1.32199"> </tspan>of<tspan data-gap="" dx="1.32199"> </tspan>the<tspan data-gap="" dx="1.32199"> </tspan>plant.<tspan data-gap="" dx="1.32199"> </tspan>They<tspan data-gap="" dx="1.32199"> </tspan>also</tspan><tspan x="89" dy="31">help support the leaf.</tspan></text>
text: Veins contain tissues that transport water and dissolved substances. They carry water into the leaf and sugars made in the leaf to other parts of the plant. They also help support the leaf.

text: In other leaves, many veins run alongside one another. This pattern is called **parallel** **venation**. In a grass blade they run along the length of the leaf. text: Janaki Ammal (1897–1984) was one of the first Indian women to work as a professional botanist. She studied sugarcane and worked on making plant varieties better. In 1952 she became Officer on Special Duty at the Botanical Survey of India and helped reorganise its work. In her eighties she joined the fight to save the forest at Silent Valley in Kerala. Her whole life was spent doing the two things this chapter is about — looking closely at plants, and finding order in what she saw.

text: Adaptations are not always about extreme places, and they are not always easy to spot. A fish has a smooth body that slips through water easily, and fins to steer and push with. html: <text class="se-copy" data-measure="874" x="89" y="174"><tspan x="89">The place where a living thing lives is called its <tspan class="se-bold">habitat</tspan>.</tspan></text>
text: The place where a living thing lives is called its **habitat**.

text: A habitat includes the conditions and resources an organism uses. Plants need light, water and minerals; animals need food as well as suitable conditions. A habitat need not be safe at all times, and an animal may use different places to feed or breed.

text: A habitat can be small: damp soil beneath a fallen log differs from the dry path beside it. Such differences help explain why nearby places can hold different living things.

html: <text class="se-copy" data-measure="874" x="89" y="445"><tspan x="89">Habitats can be sorted into two broad kinds.</tspan></text>
text: Habitats can be sorted into two broad kinds.

html: <text class="se-copy" x="89" y="494"><tspan x="89">Living things on land live in <tspan class="se-bold">terrestrial</tspan></tspan><tspan x="89" dy="31">habitats. text: Living things on land live in **terrestrial** habitats. Forests, deserts, grasslands and mountains are terrestrial habitats. So is the ground under your feet.

html: <text class="se-copy" x="542" y="494"><tspan x="542">Living things in water live in <tspan class="se-bold">aquatic</tspan></tspan><tspan x="542" dy="31">habitats. Ponds, lakes, rivers and oceans</tspan><tspan x="542" dy="31">are aquatic habitats.</tspan></text>
text: Living things in water live in **aquatic** habitats. Ponds, lakes, rivers and oceans are aquatic habitats.

A crocodile does so too, and it is a reptile.</tspan></text>
text: Some animals use both land and water. Frogs belong to a group called **amphibians**; many amphibians spend part of their lives in each. But using both habitats does not make every animal an amphibian. A crocodile does so too, and it is a reptile.

text: Salim Ali (1896–1987) spent many years travelling across India, watching birds. He recorded where they lived, when they arrived, and where they went next. Watching carefully like this, year after year, is how scattered sightings turn into real knowledge. His fieldwork and advocacy helped strengthen bird conservation in India. His books also made it possible for ordinary people to name the birds around them. He is remembered as the Birdman of India.

Rules about cutting, collecting and hunting vary. Some groves preserve old trees and habitat missing from nearby cleared land. Some also have legal protection. Find out how a grove near you is protected.

Does that record alone show that protection caused the difference?</tspan></text>
text: Suppose a class records more kinds of birds in a protected grove than in a nearby clearing. Does that record alone show that protection caused the difference?

text: Check how the records were made. Were both places watched for the same length of time, at similar times of day? Could differences in area, water or vegetation also matter?

text: Plan repeated visits using the same method. Decide what to record so another class could check your comparison. A useful conclusion must account for both the evidence and its limits.

html: <text class="se-heading" x="89" y="124"><tspan x="89">Keywords</tspan></text>
text: Keywords

html: <rect class="se-glossary-panel" x="89" y="151" width="874" height="1147" rx="20"></rect>

<text class="se-copy" x="113" y="199"><tspan x="113"><tspan class="se-bold">Adaptation</tspan> — An inherited feature</tspan><tspan x="113" dy="31">that helps an organism survive and</tspan><tspan x="113" dy="31">reproduce in its usual environment.</tspan></text>
text: **Adaptation** — An inherited feature that helps an organism survive and reproduce in its usual environment.

html: <text class="se-copy" x="113" y="304"><tspan x="113"><tspan class="se-bold">Amphibian</tspan> — An animal belonging to</tspan><tspan x="113" dy="31">the group that includes frogs and</tspan><tspan x="113" dy="31">toads; many use water and land during</tspan><tspan x="113" dy="31">their lives.</tspan></text>
text: **Amphibian** — An animal belonging to the group that includes frogs and toads; many use water and land during their lives.

html: <text class="se-copy" x="113" y="440"><tspan x="113"><tspan class="se-bold">Aquatic</tspan> — Living in water, or</tspan><tspan x="113" dy="31">describing a habitat in water.</tspan></text>
text: **Aquatic** — Living in water, or describing a habitat in water.

html: <text class="se-copy" x="113" y="514"><tspan x="113"><tspan class="se-bold">Biodiversity</tspan> — The variety of living</tspan><tspan x="113" dy="31">things found in a region.</tspan></text>
text: **Biodiversity** — The variety of living things found in a region.

html: <text class="se-copy" x="113" y="588"><tspan x="113"><tspan class="se-bold">Climber</tspan> — A plant that grows</tspan><tspan x="113" dy="31">upwards using external support.</tspan></text>
text: **Climber** — A plant that grows upwards using external support.

html: <text class="se-copy" x="113" y="662"><tspan x="113"><tspan class="se-bold">Cotyledon</tspan> — A seed leaf that is part</tspan><tspan x="113" dy="31">of the embryo inside a seed.</tspan></text>
text: **Cotyledon** — A seed leaf that is part of the embryo inside a seed.

html: <text class="se-copy" x="113" y="736"><tspan x="113"><tspan class="se-bold">Creeper</tspan> — A plant with stems that</tspan><tspan x="113" dy="31">trail along the ground.</tspan></text>
text: **Creeper** — A plant with stems that trail along the ground.

html: <text class="se-copy" x="113" y="810"><tspan x="113"><tspan class="se-bold">Dicot</tspan> — A flowering plant whose seed</tspan><tspan x="113" dy="31">has two cotyledons.</tspan></text>
text: **Dicot** — A flowering plant whose seed has two cotyledons.

html: <text class="se-copy" x="113" y="884"><tspan x="113"><tspan class="se-bold">Endosperm</tspan> — Food-storing tissue in</tspan><tspan x="113" dy="31">a seed that nourishes the developing</tspan><tspan x="113" dy="31">embryo.</tspan></text>
text: **Endosperm** — Food-storing tissue in a seed that nourishes the developing embryo.

html: <text class="se-copy" x="113" y="989"><tspan x="113"><tspan class="se-bold">Fibrous</tspan> <tspan class="se-bold">root</tspan> <tspan class="se-bold">system</tspan> — A spreading</tspan><tspan x="113" dy="31">bunch of roots without one dominant</tspan><tspan x="113" dy="31">main root.</tspan></text>
text: **Fibrous** **root** **system** — A spreading bunch of roots without one dominant main root.

html: <text class="se-copy" x="113" y="1094"><tspan x="113"><tspan class="se-bold">Grouping</tspan> — Arranging things by</tspan><tspan x="113" dy="31">features they share, using a stated</tspan><tspan x="113" dy="31">rule.</tspan></text>
text: **Grouping** — Arranging things by features they share, using a stated rule.

html: <text class="se-copy" x="113" y="1199"><tspan x="113"><tspan class="se-bold">Habitat</tspan> — The place where an</tspan><tspan x="113" dy="31">organism lives, including its</tspan><tspan x="113" dy="31">conditions and resources.</tspan></text>
text: **Habitat** — The place where an organism lives, including its conditions and resources.

html: <text class="se-copy" x="541" y="199"><tspan x="541"><tspan class="se-bold">Herb</tspan> — A plant with soft, non-woody</tspan><tspan x="541" dy="31">stems; it need not be small.</tspan></text>
text: **Herb** — A plant with soft, non-woody stems; it need not be small.

html: <text class="se-copy" x="541" y="273"><tspan x="541"><tspan class="se-bold">Monocot</tspan> — A flowering plant whose</tspan><tspan x="541" dy="31">seed has one cotyledon.</tspan></text>
text: **Monocot** — A flowering plant whose seed has one cotyledon.

html: <text class="se-copy" x="541" y="347"><tspan x="541"><tspan class="se-bold">Parallel</tspan> <tspan class="se-bold">venation</tspan> — A leaf-vein</tspan><tspan x="541" dy="31">pattern in which many veins run</tspan><tspan x="541" dy="31">alongside one another.</tspan></text>
text: **Parallel** **venation** — A leaf-vein pattern in which many veins run alongside one another.

html: <text class="se-copy" x="541" y="452"><tspan x="541"><tspan class="se-bold">Pseudostem</tspan> — A trunk-like structure</tspan><tspan x="541" dy="31">formed by overlapping leaf bases, as in</tspan><tspan x="541" dy="31">banana.</tspan></text>
text: **Pseudostem** — A trunk-like structure formed by overlapping leaf bases, as in banana.

html: <text class="se-copy" x="541" y="557"><tspan x="541"><tspan class="se-bold">Reticulate</tspan> <tspan class="se-bold">venation</tspan> — A leaf-vein</tspan><tspan x="541" dy="31">pattern in which veins branch and join</tspan><tspan x="541" dy="31">to form a network.</tspan></text>
text: **Reticulate** **venation** — A leaf-vein pattern in which veins branch and join to form a network.

html: <text class="se-copy" x="541" y="662"><tspan x="541"><tspan class="se-bold">Sacred</tspan> <tspan class="se-bold">grove</tspan> — A patch of vegetation</tspan><tspan x="541" dy="31">protected through local cultural or</tspan><tspan x="541" dy="31">religious traditions.</tspan></text>
text: **Sacred** **grove** — A patch of vegetation protected through local cultural or religious traditions.

html: <text class="se-copy" x="541" y="767"><tspan x="541"><tspan class="se-bold">Shrub</tspan> — A woody plant that usually</tspan><tspan x="541" dy="31">branches near the ground, often with</tspan><tspan x="541" dy="31">several main stems.</tspan></text>
text: **Shrub** — A woody plant that usually branches near the ground, often with several main stems.

html: <text class="se-copy" x="541" y="872"><tspan x="541"><tspan class="se-bold">Taproot</tspan> — The main root of a root</tspan><tspan x="541" dy="31">system, with smaller roots branching</tspan><tspan x="541" dy="31">from it.</tspan></text>
text: **Taproot** — The main root of a root system, with smaller roots branching from it.

html: <text class="se-copy" x="541" y="977"><tspan x="541"><tspan class="se-bold">Terrestrial</tspan> — Living on land, or</tspan><tspan x="541" dy="31">describing a habitat on land.</tspan></text>
text: **Terrestrial** — Living on land, or describing a habitat on land.

html: <text class="se-copy" x="541" y="1051"><tspan x="541"><tspan class="se-bold">Tree</tspan> — A woody plant that usually</tspan><tspan x="541" dy="31">develops a main trunk supporting a</tspan><tspan x="541" dy="31">crown of branches.</tspan></text>
text: **Tree** — A woody plant that usually develops a main trunk supporting a crown of branches.

html: <text class="se-copy" x="541" y="1156"><tspan x="541"><tspan class="se-bold">Venation</tspan> — The pattern of veins in a</tspan><tspan x="541" dy="31">leaf.</tspan></text>
text: **Venation** — The pattern of veins in a leaf.

html: <text class="se-heading" x="89" y="124"><tspan x="89">Summary</tspan></text>
text: Summary

html: <text class="se-copy" data-measure="874" x="89" y="174"><tspan x="89">•<tspan data-gap="" dx="3.79985"> </tspan>The<tspan data-gap="" dx="3.79985"> </tspan>variety<tspan data-gap="" dx="3.79985"> </tspan>of<tspan data-gap="" dx="3.79985"> </tspan>living<tspan data-gap="" dx="3.79985"> </tspan>things<tspan data-gap="" dx="3.79985"> </tspan>found<tspan data-gap="" dx="3.79985"> </tspan>in<tspan data-gap="" dx="3.79985"> </tspan>a<tspan data-gap="" dx="3.79985"> </tspan>region<tspan data-gap="" dx="3.79985"> </tspan>is<tspan data-gap="" dx="3.79985"> </tspan>called<tspan data-gap="" dx="3.79985"> </tspan>its<tspan data-gap="" dx="3.79985"> </tspan>biodiversity.<tspan data-gap="" dx="3.79985"> </tspan>Even<tspan data-gap="" dx="3.79985"> </tspan>an</tspan><tspan x="89" dy="31">ordinary place has much more of it than a quick look suggests.</tspan></text>
text: • The variety of living things found in a region is called its biodiversity. Even an ordinary place has much more of it than a quick look suggests.

html: <text class="se-copy" data-measure="874" x="89" y="264.27272727272725"><tspan x="89">• Living things in a place depend on each other for food, shelter and other needs.</tspan></text>
text: • Living things in a place depend on each other for food, shelter and other needs.

html: <text class="se-copy" data-measure="874" x="89" y="323.54545454545456"><tspan x="89">•<tspan data-gap="" dx="7.09827"> </tspan>Grouping<tspan data-gap="" dx="7.09827"> </tspan>means<tspan data-gap="" dx="7.09827"> </tspan>arranging<tspan data-gap="" dx="7.09827"> </tspan>things<tspan data-gap="" dx="7.09827"> </tspan>by<tspan data-gap="" dx="7.09827"> </tspan>the<tspan data-gap="" dx="7.09827"> </tspan>features<tspan data-gap="" dx="7.09827"> </tspan>they<tspan data-gap="" dx="7.09827"> </tspan>share.<tspan data-gap="" dx="7.09827"> </tspan>Different<tspan data-gap="" dx="7.09827"> </tspan>rules</tspan><tspan x="89" dy="31">answer different questions; each must be applied consistently.</tspan></text>
text: • Grouping means arranging things by the features they share. Different rules answer different questions; each must be applied consistently.

html: <text class="se-copy" data-measure="874" x="89" y="413.81818181818187"><tspan x="89">•<tspan data-gap="" dx="3.73579"> </tspan>Woody<tspan data-gap="" dx="3.73579"> </tspan>stems<tspan data-gap="" dx="3.73579"> </tspan>and<tspan data-gap="" dx="3.73579"> </tspan>branching<tspan data-gap="" dx="3.73579"> </tspan>help<tspan data-gap="" dx="3.73579"> </tspan>distinguish<tspan data-gap="" dx="3.73579"> </tspan>trees<tspan data-gap="" dx="3.73579"> </tspan>and<tspan data-gap="" dx="3.73579"> </tspan>shrubs<tspan data-gap="" dx="3.73579"> </tspan>from<tspan data-gap="" dx="3.73579"> </tspan>non-woody</tspan><tspan x="89" dy="31">herbs.<tspan data-gap="" dx="2.98785"> </tspan>Climbing<tspan data-gap="" dx="2.98785"> </tspan>and<tspan data-gap="" dx="2.98785"> </tspan>trailing<tspan data-gap="" dx="2.98785"> </tspan>describe<tspan data-gap="" dx="2.98785"> </tspan>growth<tspan data-gap="" dx="2.98785"> </tspan>habits,<tspan data-gap="" dx="2.98785"> </tspan>which<tspan data-gap="" dx="2.98785"> </tspan>can<tspan data-gap="" dx="2.98785"> </tspan>overlap<tspan data-gap="" dx="2.98785"> </tspan>with<tspan data-gap="" dx="2.98785"> </tspan>these</tspan><tspan x="89" dy="31">descriptions.</tspan></text>
text: • Woody stems and branching help distinguish trees and shrubs from non-woody herbs. Climbing and trailing describe growth habits, which can overlap with these descriptions.

html: <text class="se-copy" data-measure="874" x="89" y="535.0909090909091"><tspan x="89">•<tspan data-gap="" dx="7.01733"> </tspan>The<tspan data-gap="" dx="7.01733"> </tspan>pattern<tspan data-gap="" dx="7.01733"> </tspan>of<tspan data-gap="" dx="7.01733"> </tspan>veins<tspan data-gap="" dx="7.01733"> </tspan>in<tspan data-gap="" dx="7.01733"> </tspan>a<tspan data-gap="" dx="7.01733"> </tspan>leaf<tspan data-gap="" dx="7.01733"> </tspan>is<tspan data-gap="" dx="7.01733"> </tspan>called<tspan data-gap="" dx="7.01733"> </tspan>venation.<tspan data-gap="" dx="7.01733"> </tspan>Two<tspan data-gap="" dx="7.01733"> </tspan>common<tspan data-gap="" dx="7.01733"> </tspan>patterns<tspan data-gap="" dx="7.01733"> </tspan>are</tspan><tspan x="89" dy="31">reticulate and parallel.</tspan></text>
text: • The pattern of veins in a leaf is called venation. Two common patterns are reticulate and parallel.

html: <text class="se-copy" data-measure="874" x="89" y="625.3636363636364"><tspan x="89">•<tspan data-gap="" dx="0.83919"> </tspan>Two<tspan data-gap="" dx="0.83919"> </tspan>common<tspan data-gap="" dx="0.83919"> </tspan>root<tspan data-gap="" dx="0.83919"> </tspan>systems<tspan data-gap="" dx="0.83919"> </tspan>are<tspan data-gap="" dx="0.83919"> </tspan>taproot<tspan data-gap="" dx="0.83919"> </tspan>and<tspan data-gap="" dx="0.83919"> </tspan>fibrous<tspan data-gap="" dx="0.83919"> </tspan>root<tspan data-gap="" dx="0.83919"> </tspan>systems.<tspan data-gap="" dx="0.83919"> </tspan>A<tspan data-gap="" dx="0.83919"> </tspan>taproot<tspan data-gap="" dx="0.83919"> </tspan>has<tspan data-gap="" dx="0.83919"> </tspan>one</tspan><tspan x="89" dy="31">main root. Fibrous roots form a spreading bunch.</tspan></text>
text: • Two common root systems are taproot and fibrous root systems. A taproot has one main root. Fibrous roots form a spreading bunch.
